# Fugitive Wanted for Decades Captured in Wyoming After Living as Sheepherder

*By CNN Staff*

**CHEYENNE, Wyoming** — A man who had eluded federal authorities for more than 25 years was captured Tuesday in a remote stretch of Wyoming's high plains, where he had been living under an assumed identity working as a sheepherder, the FBI announced Wednesday.

Daniel Roswell Hicks, 58, had been the subject of an FBI manhunt since 1998, when he vanished following charges related to a fraud scheme that prosecutors say bilked investors out of more than $12 million. He was captured without incident at a remote grazing camp roughly 40 miles outside Sundance, Wyoming, where he had reportedly been living under the name "Wayne Cutter" for at least a decade.

"This was the product of old-fashioned investigative work combined with new forensic genealogy techniques," said FBI Special Agent in Charge Marissa Delgado, who oversaw the operation from the Denver field office. "Mr. Hicks had built an entirely new life, but persistence pays off in these cases."

## A Careful, Deliberate Approach

Given the isolated location and the fact that Hicks was known to be in possession of firearms — common among those who work in remote sheepherding operations to protect flocks from predators — federal officials say they took extensive precautions in planning the arrest.

Agency officials, speaking on background, acknowledged that the standoff at Ruby Ridge in 1992, along with the deadly siege at Waco in 1993, weighed heavily on the operational planning.

"Any time you're dealing with a rural, isolated setting involving a subject who may be armed, there's a heightened awareness of how quickly things can go wrong," said a senior FBI tactical coordinator involved in the planning, who was not authorized to speak on the record. "We studied the terrain for weeks. We wanted overwhelming information advantage, not overwhelming force."

According to officials, the FBI's Hostage Rescue Team consulted with behavioral analysts and local ranchers who knew "Cutter" personally to build a profile of his daily movements, temperament, and routine before moving in. Agents reportedly monitored the camp for nearly two weeks, waiting for a moment when Hicks was away from his firearms and had no direct line of sight to approaching vehicles.

"We were not going to have another Ruby Ridge," the tactical coordinator said. "That case is still taught at Quantico as a cautionary tale about how surveillance, communication failures, and escalation can turn a fugitive apprehension into a tragedy. Every decision here was made with that in the back of our minds."

Local Crook County Sheriff's deputies assisted with perimeter support but were kept at a distance during the actual approach, per FBI protocol, to minimize the number of armed personnel converging on the scene at once.

## Life on the Range

Neighbors and fellow herders in the sparsely populated ranching community said "Wayne Cutter" was known as quiet, reliable, and skilled with livestock, tending flocks for a large sheep operation that leases federal grazing land.

"He kept to himself, but he was good with the animals," said Russ Talbot, a rancher who employed Hicks for the past six years. "Never talked about his past. I figured maybe he had some kind of story, but you don't ask out here. A lot of guys come out to the range to get away from something."

Investigators believe Hicks moved through several Western states in the years following his disappearance, taking on itinerant agricultural work that required little documentation and paid in cash, before settling into the sheepherding job in northeastern Wyoming.

## Charges and Next Steps

Hicks has been transported to Denver, where he will face the original 1998 federal charges, including wire fraud, money laundering, and failure to appear. Prosecutors say additional charges related to identity theft — for allegedly assuming the identity of a deceased Montana man to obtain his "Wayne Cutter" documents — are also likely.

The FBI's Denver field office said the case underscores the bureau's continued willingness to pursue decades-old fugitive cases using new technology, including facial recognition software and DNA genealogy databases that have cracked open a number of cold cases in recent years.

"Time doesn't run out on a warrant," Delgado said. "We are exceedingly patient, and increasingly good at finding people who think they've disappeared."

Hicks is expected to make his first court appearance in federal court in Denver later this week.

# Fugitive Wanted in Mississippi Homicide Captured in Rural Wyoming After Weeks-Long FBI Manhunt

**WORLAND, Wyo.** — A man wanted in connection with a homicide investigation in Mississippi was apprehended Thursday by FBI agents in a remote area of Washakie County, ending a multi-state manhunt that had stretched on for nearly six weeks, authorities said.

Edward Eugene Harper, 47, was taken into custody without incident shortly before dawn at a rural property roughly 15 miles outside Worland, according to a statement released by the FBI's Denver Field Office, which coordinated the operation with the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation and local law enforcement.

"This was the result of tireless work by multiple agencies across several states," said Special Agent in Charge Melissa Grant. "Harper believed he could disappear into rural America. He was wrong."

## A Cross-Country Flight

Harper had been the subject of a federal warrant since early last month, when he allegedly fled Mississippi after being named a suspect in the death of a 39-year-old man in Lauderdale County. Local prosecutors there said they intended to charge Harper with second-degree murder, though he vanished before charges could be formally filed.

Investigators said Harper's trail went cold for weeks before tips began trickling in suggesting he had made his way through Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Colorado before settling into the sparsely populated ranchland of northern Wyoming, where he allegedly took on manual labor jobs under an assumed name.

"These cases test patience as much as they test investigative skill," said DCI Special Agent Tom Reyes, who assisted in the search. "Washakie County isn't a place people typically associate with fugitive recovery operations, but that isolation is exactly what made it attractive to him — and ultimately what made him easier to isolate."

## The Takedown

Acting on a tip from a local resident who recognized Harper from a regional bulletin, agents established surveillance on a secluded property Wednesday evening. A tactical team moved in before sunrise Thursday, arresting Harper as he attempted to leave the residence in a pickup truck.

No shots were fired, and no injuries were reported. Officials said Harper offered minimal resistance.

"He knew it was over," one agent involved in the arrest told reporters at the scene, speaking on condition of anonymity because the case remains active.

## What Comes Next

Harper is currently being held at a federal detention facility in Casper pending an extradition hearing. Mississippi authorities have confirmed they will seek his return to face charges in the homicide case.

The FBI has not released additional details about Harper's activities during his time at large, citing the ongoing investigation. Officials also declined to say whether Harper will face additional federal charges related to his flight from prosecution, though fleeing to avoid prosecution across state lines can itself constitute a federal offense.

Family members of the victim in Mississippi released a brief statement through their attorney thanking investigators "for their persistence in bringing him home to face justice."

The FBI said the case underscores the bureau's continued reliance on public tips in fugitive investigations. "Even in the most remote corners of the country, someone is paying attention," Grant said. "That's often the difference-maker in cases like this."

---
*This story is developing and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Tense Standoff in Big Horn Mountains Ends Peacefully as FBI Captures Fugitive

**BUFFALO, Wyo.** — After nine days tracking a wanted man through the rugged terrain of the Big Horn Mountains, FBI agents brought the manhunt to a peaceful close Tuesday afternoon, arresting 47-year-old Dale Whitmore without a single shot fired—a resolution that agency officials credited to lessons learned from past standoffs gone tragically wrong.

Whitmore, wanted on federal weapons charges and accused of firing on state troopers during a traffic stop near Sheridan earlier this month, had retreated into the high country with what investigators believed was a substantial cache of firearms. The combination of his military background, his professed anti-government views, and the unforgiving terrain of the Bighorn National Forest created what one agent called "a powder keg scenario"—the kind of situation that has haunted federal law enforcement for more than three decades.

## The Shadow of Ruby Ridge

Agents on scene didn't need reminding of what can go wrong. The 1992 siege at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, remains a cautionary touchstone within the Bureau—a case study taught in training academies and referenced quietly among veteran agents whenever a standoff involves armed, isolated individuals with deep distrust of federal authority.

That confrontation, which began as an attempt to arrest Randy Weaver on weapons charges, spiraled into an 11-day siege that left Weaver's wife, teenage son, and a U.S. Marshal dead. The tragedy became a rallying point for anti-government militia movements and prompted sweeping reforms in how federal agencies approach armed standoffs, particularly rules of engagement and command structure.

"Nobody out here forgot Ruby Ridge," said Special Agent in Charge Marcus Delaney, who oversaw the operation from a command post established at a ranch near the base of the mountains. "That's not ancient history to us. It's the reason we do things differently now."

Those differences were evident throughout the operation. Rather than surrounding Whitmore's suspected position with an overwhelming show of force, agents established a wide perimeter and relied on aerial surveillance, patience, and negotiation.

## A Measured Approach

For over a week, a specialized crisis negotiation team attempted repeated radio contact with Whitmore, who had abandoned his vehicle near Hunter Corrals and continued on foot into increasingly remote terrain. Agents tracked him through Elk Camp Draw and toward the granite faces below Cloud Peak, adjusting their perimeter each time he moved.

"Every decision was made with an eye toward de-escalation," said Delaney. "We were not going to back him into a corner. We were not going to give him a reason to believe his life was in immediate danger, because history tells us what happens when a scared, armed person believes that."

Local ranchers were evacuated from a five-mile radius as a precaution, and Bighorn National Forest officials closed several popular trailheads, including access points near Coffeen Park and the West Tensleep trailhead, drawing frustration from hikers but little public criticism given the circumstances.

Weather nearly complicated the operation on its sixth day, when an early autumn storm dropped several inches of snow above 9,000 feet, temporarily grounding surveillance aircraft. Ground teams, working in coordination with local sheriff's deputies familiar with the terrain, maintained containment through the whiteout conditions.

## The Arrest

The breakthrough came not through confrontation, but exhaustion and communication. On the ninth day, negotiators reestablished radio contact after Whitmore's satellite phone—supplied earlier in the standoff by agents as a gesture of good faith—registered movement toward a lower elevation.

According to FBI accounts, Whitmore indicated he was willing to surrender if guaranteed he would not be shot on sight, a fear negotiators worked to address directly, referencing the department's explicit commitment to a peaceful resolution.

At approximately 2:15 p.m., Whitmore emerged from a stand of lodgepole pines near the Paint Rock drainage, hands visible, and was taken into custody without incident. Agents recovered two rifles and a handgun from his position; no injuries were reported on either side.

## Reflection, Not Celebration

Bureau officials were notably restrained in their public statements, avoiding any language that might suggest triumph over tragedy narrowly avoided.

"This is what success looks like," Delaney told reporters at a brief press conference in Buffalo. "Nobody died. Nobody got hurt. A wanted man is in custody and will face the justice system. That's the outcome we work for every time, and it's the outcome we didn't always get right in this country's past."

Legal experts noted that the FBI's handling of the Whitmore case will likely be studied alongside other successful de-escalations as evidence that institutional reforms following Ruby Ridge—and later, the Waco siege—have meaningfully changed federal tactics.

Whitmore was transported to Sheridan for arraignment on federal charges including assault on law enforcement officers and unlawful possession of firearms. His attorney did not respond to requests for comment.

For residents of Johnson County, the standoff's quiet resolution offered relief tempered by unease—a reminder of how quickly isolated mountain terrain can become the backdrop for confrontations with stakes far beyond the individual involved.

"We were scared something bad was going to happen," said Ellen Marsh, a rancher whose property bordered part of the perimeter. "I'm just glad these folks seemed like they were trying not to let that happen."

# FBI Uses Wildlife Ruse to Capture Sovereign Citizen Fugitive Without Incident

Federal authorities have successfully apprehended a fugitive linked to the sovereign citizen movement using an elaborate ruse involving fake wildlife officer credentials, ending a standoff that could have turned violent.

The suspect, wanted on outstanding warrants in Mississippi, had evaded law enforcement for an extended period, adopting the ideology common among sovereign citizens who reject the legitimacy of federal and state government authority. Individuals within this movement have historically presented significant risks to arresting officers, sometimes refusing to recognize the authority of badges or warrants and, in some cases, responding with force.

Aware of these risks, FBI agents devised an alternative approach rather than attempting a conventional confrontational arrest. Investigators determined that the fugitive was known to interact cooperatively with wildlife and conservation officers, likely due to his interests or activities in rural or wooded areas.

Capitalizing on this behavioral pattern, agents disguised themselves as state wildlife officers, complete with credentials and equipment designed to pass casual inspection. The approach allowed agents to close the distance and engage directly with the suspect without triggering the defensive or hostile posture often associated with sovereign citizen encounters involving recognized law enforcement.

The ruse worked precisely as intended. The suspect, believing he was speaking with wildlife officials rather than federal agents, was taken into custody without incident. No shots were fired, no injuries were reported, and the arrest was completed peacefully.

Following his apprehension, the fugitive was processed and has since been extradited to Mississippi, where he will face the pending charges outlined in his original warrants.

Law enforcement officials have noted that creative, non-confrontational tactics like this are increasingly employed when dealing with individuals who hold anti-government beliefs, as such approaches can significantly reduce the risk of violence for both suspects and officers. The successful outcome of this operation underscores the value of behavioral intelligence and tactical creativity in modern fugitive apprehension efforts.

The FBI has not released the fugitive's identity or additional details about the specific charges pending against him in Mississippi, citing ongoing legal proceedings.
